exp_mews_squad_title: Squad Lead — Experience team, Growth tribe
exp_mews_squad_blurb: Led a cross-functional squad on the experience layer of the PMS: an entirely new product navigation and key upgrades to the assistant search. Built the navigation package behind it — route-active detection, enterprise-scoped links, TanStack Router and Query — as its main author, and rolled it out behind feature flags one surface at a time. Planned the work, ran the ceremonies and mentored junior engineers while remaining the team's main delivery engineer, and introduced AI-assisted workflows and tooling that cut the repetitive work.
exp_mews_techlead_title: Tech Lead — Design System team, DX Platform tribe
exp_mews_techlead_blurb: Set the technical direction for the design systems behind a large product's UI as their formal code owner: the established library of ~102 components that some 81 packages consume, its new-generation replacement — where I am the top author of the core — and the guest-facing one. The flagship delivery was its DataGrid: filtering, URL-synced state, grouping and accessibility, designed as one component API rather than a screen, and now the default for every data-heavy screen in the product. Owned components end to end besides, from API design to docs, Storybook and tests — the SideMenu and the useSideMenu hook it exposes serve the PMS and the Events Management System from a single source. And drove a sustained accessibility push across the system: ARIA, keyboard navigation, focus management and screen-reader support, backed by axe-based tests.
exp_mews_senior_title: Senior Software Engineer — Design System team, DX Platform tribe
exp_mews_senior_blurb: Shipped component libraries and frontend tooling for a large React/TypeScript monorepo — over four years I became its third most frequent contributor of 713, across some 717 pull requests. Second human contributor to the multi-brand design-tokens pipeline (Figma → Token Studio → Style Dictionary), where one source of truth drives four brand themes on web and Android. Partnered closely with product engineers, offering hands-on support, and with the Platform Productivity team to improve developer experience across the board.
exp_liferay_blurb: Product engineer on Liferay DXP — the enterprise digital-experience platform — building and shipping rich new features, most notably for the 7.4 release, with React, Clay, portlets and a healthy measure of Java. Beyond the code, I helped shape the roadmap with product owners and improve team workflows with project managers.
exp_docline_blurb: Led the frontend of a telemedicine platform, taking its Vue codebase to the next level — component reusability, best practices, and large-scale refactors, including introducing an app-wide shared store as the single source of truth for application state. Reviewed architecture, standardised code reviews, fostered a strong team culture, and improved the existing design system across Vue, TS and SCSS.
exp_indra_po_title: Product Owner & Engineer — Onesait platform website
exp_indra_po_blurb: Owned and delivered the main web app promoting Onesait products, bridging engineering and marketing. Led a team of four engineers and one designer, managing multiple stakeholders.
exp_indra_consultant_title: Senior Software Engineer & Consultant — Onesait Design System
exp_indra_consultant_blurb: Main delivery engineer on the Vue.js-based design system, and the go-to reference supporting every product engineering team adopting it.
exp_ironhack_blurb: Taught intensive full-stack web development bootcamps. Fast-paced and hands-on — and nothing hones your own fundamentals quite like teaching them to others.
exp_tau_blurb: Led a team of up to six developers at a design-led agency — client-facing work, pitching, and mentoring juniors — delivering marketing and corporate sites, e-commerce stores, and a steady stream of microsites for clients like Edelvives, ECAM, Universidad Autónoma, Mapfre and Telefónica. In a studio that lived and breathed design, the bar was pixel-perfect: high-craft UI, rich interactions, and truly responsive layouts, on a jQuery, PHP and WordPress stack with SCSS and Node tooling.
exp_aulacm_blurb: Helped build and maintain the company's main site and the client websites delivered by its agency arm — my first taste of agency work and shipping custom WordPress in PHP. Doubled as the in-house WordPress instructor, teaching plugins, themes, styling and the PHP basics that make it all tick — and learning plenty the honest way myself.
exp_prev_blurb: A parallel life in sound, from around 2004 — production and post for film and TV. Two Goyas for documentaries, a Berlinale run after three weeks filming with orphans in Kenya, and a good showing at festivals besides; behind the desk, a Pro Tools wizard and Final Cut obsessive fluent in Avalon compressors, Neve preamps and a wall of top-notch mics. With my friend Iván I built lacasaestudio — still alive and thriving — and the instincts stuck: precision, grace under live pressure, reading a room, and tight teamwork.

ui_cs_code_private: The code is private — happy to walk through it on a call.
cs_billing_intro: A billing engine that repays cash advances by taking a share of a merchant's daily revenue, driven day by day against a live API across a simulated month. It began as a take-home exercise, which is why the source stays private — I'm happy to walk anyone through it.
cs_billing_n1_h: One backlog, not three code paths
cs_billing_n1_b: Revenue that arrives late, a daily charge cap, and a charge the processor rejects look like three problems. They are one: an amount that could not settle today. Each advance carries a backlog, all three feed it, and the next day drains it under the same rules. The hard part of the brief turned out to be small once it had the right name.
cs_billing_n2_b: Amounts arrive as two-decimal strings, parsed once at the edge into a branded integer type and formatted once on the way out. The arithmetic in between goes through helpers that re-validate, so a float can never reach a balance. Rounding happens in exactly one place, and is documented because the spec was silent on it.
cs_billing_n3_h: A port, so every edge case is provable
cs_billing_n3_b: A live API cannot be asked to reject a charge or withhold a day's revenue on demand. One interface with two implementations — the real client and an in-memory fake — turns each failure mode into a deterministic test. All 136 of them run offline, in seconds.
cs_billing_n4_h: Decisions written down where the spec was silent
cs_billing_n4_b: Rounding, the accrual window, what becomes of an advance that cannot repay before the period ends, whether the daily cap is per advance or per mandate: each chosen once, pinned by a test, and listed with its reasoning. An architecture decision record covers the alternatives rejected — including the monorepo that would have demonstrated more and proved less.
cs_billing_shot1_alt: The run report: outstanding portfolio balance, collection statistics and every advance in the run.
cs_billing_shot1_cap: Each run writes a self-contained HTML report — no server, no build step, opens from disk.
cs_billing_shot2_alt: One advance's event ledger, showing eight consecutive rejected charges.
cs_billing_shot2_cap: An advance whose mandate stopped working. The balance stays intact and a human gets told; “stalled” is a reporting diagnosis, never a state the domain invents.
proj_billing_desc: A daily billing engine for cash advances: a pure domain core behind a ports-and-adapters seam, with late revenue, daily caps and rejected charges all carried forward by one mechanism.
proj_perico_desc: A translator that rewrites plain Spanish in the voice of a cycling commentator — retrieval, evaluation, and a 20-part course documenting how it was built.
cs_ensayadero_tagline: A rehearsal room that listens back.
cs_ensayadero_intro: Drop in a recording of the band and it comes back split into stems, with a MIDI file for each pitched instrument and a chord chart the band can edit. A multi-track mixer plays it all together — mute and solo, loop markers, per-instrument MIDI synths — so you can loop the four bars everyone keeps getting wrong. In invite-only beta.
cs_ensayadero_n1_h: Every model runs on my own hardware
cs_ensayadero_n1_b: No paid inference. The web app spawns a Python CLI — Demucs for separation, Basic Pitch and Omnizart for transcription — as a detached process behind an in-memory queue capped at two workers, so two uploads never fight over the same machine. Because that queue lives in memory, a boot reconciler re-queues whatever was left mid-processing when the container restarts, with an attempts cap so a poisoned job cannot loop forever.
cs_ensayadero_n2_h: Chord detection that admits what it doesn't know
cs_ensayadero_n2_b: Omnizart first, then madmom, then a template derived from the MIDI — major and minor only. Three models that disagree produce a starting point, not an answer, so the chart is editable and the band's corrections survive reprocessing. Naming the uncertainty in the UI was cheaper and more honest than chasing a fourth model.
cs_perico_tagline: A translator with a very specific voice.
cs_perico_intro: Paste ordinary Spanish and it comes back in the voice of Perico Delgado — Tour winner turned commentator, famous for mangling a proverb halfway through. Results stream over server-sent events, with speech synthesis and dictation. Every stage of building it is written up as a twenty-part public course. The corpus behind it is personal study material and is not published.
cs_perico_n1_h: The configuration value that was secretly the experiment
cs_perico_n1_b: RETRIEVE_N = 12 looked like a tuning knob. It was the whole question: can twelve retrieved phrases beat the fifty hand-picked ones already in the prompt? Framed that way, retrieval was losing by construction. Finding that out needed an evaluation suite — a blind judge, retrieval self-recall, repetition rate, and a configuration sweep with error bars — rather than an opinion about whether the output felt right.
cs_perico_n2_b: pytest is scoped to tests/ and nothing under evals/ is named test_*, because those scripts call a paid API — a bare pytest must not be able to run up a bill. Production installs from a requirements file generated out of the manifest rather than one kept by hand, so the 1.4 GB of local ML that the corpus tools need never reaches the server. The two drifted apart once; generating it means they cannot again.
cs_tartaytantas_tagline: A bakery's shop window, and the desk behind it.
cs_tartaytantas_intro: The online cake shop for my sister's workshop in Madrid: a public catalogue, and a Spanish-language back office where she manages products, allergens, holidays and delivery rules herself. Checkout runs through Snipcart, with delivery-date rules and distance-based shipping.
cs_tartaytantas_n1_h: Server-rendered so an edit is live on the next request
cs_tartaytantas_n1_b: Product pages render on the server rather than being statically built with a rebuild hook. She changes a price and it is live immediately — no deploy, nothing to explain, nothing for me to be on call for.
cs_tartaytantas_n2_h: A handover runbook, because the site is not mine
cs_tartaytantas_n2_b: A nine-step ownership cutover across GitHub, Vercel, Supabase, Google Cloud, Snipcart, Stripe and the domain, written as one Markdown source rendered into a tickable checklist. Access is layered underneath it — row-level security on every table, an allow-list of emails, roles, and a guard that refuses to delete or demote the last remaining admin.
cs_triscaideca_tagline: Forty-two projects, published from a WeTransfer folder.
cs_triscaideca_intro: A portfolio for an interior-architecture studio: a grid wall where each project declares its own column span, row span and height, detail pages with sliders, and a contact map. Content is one JSON file per project — no CMS, because nobody was going to log into one.
cs_triscaideca_n1_h: The interesting part is the publishing pipeline
cs_triscaideca_n1_b: Two scripted workflows turn the studio's actual delivery format into a site update: read the project metadata out of the RTF they write, find the folder the photographer sent, resize every image to 1600px and around 220 KB, renumber them, shift every existing project's order so the new one lands first, and write the JSON. Publishing a project went from an afternoon to a command.
cs_triscaideca_n2_b: The stack is old and staying there. It is hosted on Netlify because Netlify still runs Node 16 and Vercel does not — the hosting follows the constraint instead of fighting it. The setup notes go down to the sharp edges, including the Python version a native dependency needs to compile on Apple Silicon.
cs_paellalab_tagline: The arithmetic behind a good rice.
cs_paellalab_intro: Pan diameter and number of people in; broth, rice, fat, salt and timings out, modelling how much water a given pan loses to evaporation. Around the calculator: recipes, a registry of your own pans, a timer and a cooking assistant. Installable, offline-capable, bilingual.
cs_paellalab_n1_h: A small assistant on cheap inference
cs_paellalab_n1_b: Embeddings from Hugging Face, vector search in Postgres, generation on Groq, with rate limiting written into the route itself — a hundred messages a day, ten a minute — sized for roughly fifteen users. A frontier model would have cost more per month than the app is worth, and would not have answered a question about rice any better.
cs_paellalab_n2_b: Only authentication and navigation load eagerly; every landing section waits until it is visible. The gated content exists twice on purpose — enforced on the server, softened on the client with a fade — because the first is the rule and the second is the manners.
cs_carabanchel_tagline: A neighbourhood, mapped by the people living in it.
cs_carabanchel_intro: An interactive map of the cultural and commercial fabric of Carabanchel, in Madrid, built with the IED: editors publish collections through a CMS and the public app draws them as layers over Mapbox — local commerce, the people who sustain it, and the places at risk of disappearing. A collaboration, not a solo build.
cs_carabanchel_n1_b: Rather than storing loose latitude and longitude columns, a feature's geometry is a dynamic zone built from GeoJSON components. A non-technical editor fills in a form and the API emits a valid FeatureCollection the map consumes directly — plus bulk import for the collections that arrived as files, and regeneration on save.
cs_carabanchel_n2_h: A composed map, and lists that stay smooth
cs_carabanchel_n2_b: Mapbox GL runs under Leaflet rather than standalone, which kept the plugin ecosystem available, and the side panel virtualises its feature list so a collection of hundreds of points scrolls without dropping frames on the phones people actually walk around with.
